meta.title: The Result You Already Know
meta.theme: why a well-built experiment includes a condition whose outcome is settled in advance, and what a failure there means
meta.learning_objective: fill an example slot with an instance the following sentence can point at, rather than with the generalisation the instance is meant to support

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. A general account of controls in experimental design; no specific study or text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: The sentence after the gap says 'If nothing dies on that plate', which needs a plate to have been put on the bench. Two options now supply one, and the second supplies the wrong kind: a blind reader had solved an earlier draft by taking the only concrete option, so the untreated-plate decoy was written to remove that shortcut and make the direction of the control do the work.

quality.adversarial_review: The live rival is the untreated plate, which is concrete, supplies an antecedent for 'that plate', and describes a precaution any laboratory really does take. It is killed by the sentence after the gap: on an untreated plate nothing dying is the wanted result, so 'if nothing dies on that plate the day's results are void' becomes nonsense, and the previous sentence asked for a condition in which something is already known to happen, which is the opposite device. The option about negative results being under-reported is right about the paragraph's world but belongs after the argument rather than inside it.

sentences: A negative result is ambiguous in a way a positive one is not: the effect may be absent, or the apparatus may simply have failed to register anything at all.
The remedy is to run, alongside the test itself, a condition in which something is already known to happen.
If nothing dies on that plate, the day's results are not negative; they are void.

question.stem: Which of the following sentences best fills the gap in the paragraph?

options.A: This is why the absence of an effect is reported so much less often, and so much less confidently, than the presence of one, in almost any field.
options.B: A laboratory testing whether a compound kills a bacterium puts a known antibiotic on a third plate, to see whether a death can show at all.
options.C: The same laboratory will also put out a plate with nothing added to it at all, to check that the bacterium does not simply die unaided.
options.D: Every well-designed study checks its own instruments first, though fields differ in how openly they report the checks that they ran.

explanation.what_the_gap_needs: The second sentence states the remedy in the abstract, and the sentence after the gap says 'If nothing dies on that plate', pointing at a plate and at a death. Neither has been mentioned. The gap must therefore be the concrete instance that supplies both, and it must be an instance of the remedy just described — a condition included because its outcome is already known.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option puts the abstract remedy on a bench. It introduces the third plate the next sentence points at and gives that plate a known outcome, a death, which is precisely what the next sentence's 'nothing dies' negates. The antibiotic is not there to be tested, since its effect is already known; it is there so that the plates can be asked whether they are capable of showing anything, which is the remedy the previous sentence described.

distractors.why_wrong: The under-reporting of negative results belongs to this paragraph's subject but comes after the argument is complete, not in the middle of it; placed here it leaves the following sentence pointing at a plate that no sentence has put on the bench.
distractors.seductive_element: It picks up the first sentence about the ambiguity of negative results and reads as a thoughtful development of it.

distractors.why_wrong: This is a control of the other kind — a plate on which nothing is expected to happen — so it is not an instance of the remedy just described, which was a condition in which something is already known to happen; and it makes the next sentence absurd, since nothing dying on an untreated plate is the result the laboratory is hoping for rather than a void day.
distractors.seductive_element: It is concrete, it puts a plate on the bench for the following sentence to point at, and an untreated plate is a real and familiar precaution.

distractors.why_wrong: It widens a specific point about interpreting negative results into a claim about every well-designed study in every field, and supplies neither the plate nor the known outcome the next sentence depends on.
distractors.seductive_element: It concedes that fields differ, which reads as scrupulous, and its breadth makes it feel like the sentence a serious methodological paragraph would contain.

explanation.method: An example slot is verified by the sentence after it, and by more than a demonstrative. Ask which option puts the named thing into the paragraph — 'that plate' — and then ask whether the sentence still makes sense with that thing in place. Two candidates can both supply a plate; only one makes 'if nothing dies on it, the day is void' a sensible thing to say.

mentor.challenge: The sentence after the gap points at a plate. Nothing so far has put one on the bench, and only one option does.
mentor.takeaway: Where the next sentence says 'that', the gap has to have introduced the thing. A definition is not an introduction.
